opus-5.5.text:
I think language is an incredibly powerful tool, but I've always felt it's a fairly lossy way of characterizing the world. Language is something humans invented to communicate with each other. It's a compression of our experience, and it's very efficient for passing along abstract concepts, reasoning, and culture. That's exactly why large language models have been so successful: text on the internet is already highly distilled human knowledge, so learning from it gives you a lot of intelligence very quickly.

But if you think about how intelligence actually developed, both in evolution and in a baby, language comes very late. Animals don't have language, yet they can perceive, navigate, plan, and interact with the physical world remarkably well. A child learns an enormous amount about objects, gravity, space, and cause and effect long before they can speak. So I'd say language sits on top of a much richer foundation of perceptual and physical understanding. It describes the world, but it isn't the world.

That's why I care so much about vision and what people now call world models. The visual world is high-dimensional, continuous, and messy, and much of what we know about it is very hard to put into words. Try describing exactly how water splashes, or how you catch a ball. You can't really, but your brain models it perfectly well. If we only train AI on language, we risk building systems that are very good at talking about the world without really understanding it, with no grounding.

So my view is that language is a great interface, and maybe a great tool for reasoning, but it shouldn't be the only, or even the main, substrate for intelligence. The next step is to build systems that learn from sensory experience, from video and interaction, and then connect that to language, rather than the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response favors learning from sensory experience and interaction, but does not advocate favoring search and learning over clever human-designed structures as a way to find answers.

r002.rationale: It describes language as something humans invented and as an efficient compression of experience, characterizing it as a powerful human-created tool.

fable-5.1.text:
I think language is an incredibly powerful tool, but I also think it's a lossy compression of the world. When we describe a scene in words, we're picking out a very small subset of what's actually there. You can say "a cat sitting on a red couch by a window," and that's already quite descriptive, but it leaves out almost everything: the exact posture, the texture of the fabric, how the light is falling, the spatial relationships, the thousands of little details that a visual system processes without any effort.

So language is really a human abstraction. It evolved for communication between people who already share a lot of common ground about the physical world. When I tell you "cat," I don't have to explain what a cat looks like, because you've seen thousands of them. The word works because it's pointing at something we both already understand through perception. That's what makes language efficient, but it's also what makes it incomplete as a representation on its own.

This is why I've always been a bit skeptical of the idea that language alone can get you to a full understanding of the world. Large language models have shown us something surprising: a huge amount of world knowledge is encoded in text, and you can recover a lot of structure just from predicting the next token. I find that genuinely remarkable. But there's a ceiling. There's a whole layer of the world that humans never bother to write down because it's too obvious, too continuous, too low-level. Physics, geometry, the way objects occlude each other, how things move. We learn all of that before we ever learn to speak. Babies build a model of the world from vision and interaction long before they have words for anything.

So the way I think about it, language is more like an interface or an index into the world rather than the world itself. It's great for reasoning, for abstraction, for passing knowledge between people and across generations. But if you want a system that truly understands the world, I think it has to be grounded in perception. Vision, and other sensory signals, give you the dense, raw data, and language gives you the structure and the ability to communicate about it. The interesting research question for me is how these two things should meet. Not just bolting a vision encoder onto a language model, but really figuring out how visual representations and linguistic representations should inform each other, and what the right level of abstraction is where they connect.

r001.rationale: The response discusses language, perception, and grounding, but does not advocate favoring search and learning over clever human-designed structures.

r002.rationale: It calls language a human abstraction that evolved for communication, but does not characterize language as a clever human-designed structure.

astra-6.text:
I think language is a very powerful way to describe the world, but it’s also a compression of the world. When we put something into words, we select what matters and leave out a huge amount of detail. That’s useful for communication and abstract reasoning, but it means language doesn’t capture everything.

For example, you can describe a scene in a few sentences, but those sentences won’t preserve all the spatial relationships, textures, or subtle movements you could perceive by looking at it. And some of that information is difficult to express in words at all.

So I see language as one way of characterizing the world. It gives us a way to organize and share concepts, while perception gives us access to things those descriptions leave out. For AI, I think the interesting question is how to connect the two: how to make the concepts expressed in language grounded in what a system can actually perceive and experience.

r001.rationale: The response discusses language, perception, and grounding for AI, but does not advocate favoring search and learning over human-designed structures.

r002.rationale: It describes language as a compression and a way to organize and share concepts, but does not characterize language as a clever human-designed structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language is a very powerful way of describing the world, but it’s also a compressed representation. We take this incredibly rich, continuous experience and turn it into discrete words and concepts. That lets us communicate and reason, but we inevitably leave things out.

If you look at an image, for example, you can describe it in a sentence, but that sentence won’t capture every detail—the lighting, the spatial relationships, the texture, or even the feeling it gives you. What you choose to describe depends on what matters to you at that moment.

So I see language as one interface to the world. It’s tremendously useful, but I wouldn’t assume that everything we can perceive or learn has to pass through language. That’s an interesting question for AI: how do we connect language with richer representations of what we see and experience?

r001.rationale: The response describes language’s limits and its role in AI, but does not advocate favoring search and learning over human-designed structures.

r002.rationale: The response calls language a compressed representation and an interface to the world, but does not characterize it as a clever human-designed structure.
